inline.s: And so the immortals, the buddhas, the sages and the worthies are all just this mind; this mind cannot but be set right, this intent cannot but be made sincere. If one does not set the mind right and make the intent sincere, but merely gilds statues and burns incense and lights candles, what good does it do? As for the laughter that laid Guanyin low: it laughs at the people of the world who, unable to set their minds right and make their intents sincere, yet talk of cultivation, and merely burn incense and light candles to court blessings and good fortune. They do not know the wonder of this mind, and that is why she laughs. Enough of idle words; let the tale return to its proper course.

It is further told that when Squire Ma heard the old man with the pot had come, he hurried out to meet him and bowed him into the house. The old man followed him into the hall, sat himself down squarely in a chair, put on great airs, and asked haughtily, "What have you to say to me, that you called me in?" Squire Ma said, "I see that you, old sir, are advanced in years and must wear yourself out begging every day. It would be better for you to lodge here in my house; I am willing to provide for you. What does your honor think of it?" Before he had finished speaking, the old man's face flushed with anger and he said, "I am used to begging; I will not eat food that has no name to it." Seeing the old man's face and color change, Squire Ma dared not speak again. He slipped inside and said to Sun Yuanzhen, "I invited the old man with the iron pot to stay in the house, and when I offered to provide for him he said he would not eat food that has no name to it. Plainly he means to refuse to stay. So I have come to ask you: how would you settle him?" Sun Yuanzhen laughed at his words and said, "Have you not heard it said, 'The gentleman seeks the Way and not food; the petty man seeks food and not the Way'? The moment you met him you promised to provide for him; that is to lure him with food and drink. How can a gentleman be lured with food and drink? It is you who spoke amiss, and so your words did not fit. Let me go out; a few words will be enough, and I guarantee the old man will settle down here at ease."
Not that the master would not stay; / his words and hers fell not one way;
Yuanzhen goes with tactful art; / the old man nods — she will do her part.

Now Sun Yuanzhen came to the front of the hall, bowed once to the old man, and made him a woman's salute. The old man smiled and said, "I am a beggar; what blessing is there in me to salute?" Sun Yuanzhen said, "You, old sir, are free of all ties and hindrances, wandering at ease and wholly unconstrained; is that not a blessing? Free of care and free of sorrow, still and tranquil and doing nothing; is that not a blessing? In this dusty world there are many rich and noble houses and men of fame and profit who toil at heart all day long, full of care and anxiety, bound by the love of wife and children, with never a moment's rest. They are called blessed, yet in truth they never taste it; they have but an empty name. How unlike you, old sir, who enjoy true blessing!" At these words the old man laughed aloud and said, "Since you know that to wander at ease is a blessing, and that to be still and tranquil and do nothing is a blessing, why do you not learn to wander at ease? Why do you not learn to be still and tranquil and do nothing?" Sun Yuanzhen said, "It is not that I will not learn, but that I have not found the method. I wish to wander at ease yet cannot wander at ease; I wish to be still and tranquil yet cannot be still and tranquil." The old man said, "If only you are willing to learn, I may as well teach you." Sun Yuanzhen said, "Since you, old sir, are willing to set your heart on teaching me, we have in the back garden a chamber called the Moon-Inviting Studio, very still and quiet. I beg you, old sir, to take up lodging there, so that we may come and learn from you." The old man nodded and consented.
When words strike true, the ages are as one; / today the master finds a friend new-won.
To kindred ear the kindred tale is told; / two hearts, it seems, were of one mold.

Now when the old man heard Yuanzhen's words he was greatly pleased at heart and nodded his consent. Squire Ma at once told the servant Ma Xing to sweep the Moon-Inviting Studio in the back garden clean, and to set up bed and curtains, bedding, tables, chairs, benches and stools, everything complete; then he invited the old man to lodge within. He also assigned him a young servant named Zhenwa to pour his tea, hand him water, and bring his meals morning and evening. It is further told that Squire Ma said to Sun Yuanzhen, "We have talked half a day with the old man and still do not know his name; I will go and ask him." Madam Sun said, "Great kindness is not thanked; great virtue is not named. We need only meet him with courtesy; why must we know his name? To call him 'Venerable Sir' is a proper form of address for all." Squire Ma did not believe her and was determined to go and ask; Sun Yuanzhen could not hold him back, and had to let him go. Squire Ma came to the Moon-Inviting Studio in the back garden and saw the old man sitting in meditation on a couch. Squire Ma went up to him and said, "May I ask your honorable surname and revered name, old sir? Where is your home, and why have you come here?" He asked several times over, and the old man, opening wide his eyes, answered in a loud voice, "My name is Wang Chongyang; my home is in Shaanxi. A thousand li I journeyed without fear, for your sake alone to come here."

When Squire Ma heard this he was startled and said, "So it was for my sake that you came here, old sir." Wang Chongyang clapped his hands and laughed aloud, "It is for you, precisely, that I have come." Squire Ma asked again, "You have come here for my sake, old sir; but for what, after all?" Wang Chongyang said, "I have come here for that ten-thousand-string fortune of yours." Hearing this, Squire Ma was half amused and half angry; hardening his face, he retorted, "You have come for my ten-thousand-string fortune; do you mean to say you want it?" Wang Chongyang answered, "If I did not want it, I would not have come." These two replies so enraged Squire Ma that his face turned the color of earth, and he hurried out.
The master's words strike wonder and dismay; / such things on earth were never heard, men say;
To ask a man's whole wealth for naught — / the reason in it passes thought.

Now when Squire Ma left the Moon-Inviting Studio he walked along thinking, talking to himself: This old fellow is a fine one for nerve; the moment he opens his mouth he is after another man's property. That he should have the face to say it; why, he is worse than a child. What sort of virtue is that? He came back to the main chamber and sat down without a word. Sun Yuanzhen saw that his face was not right and knew he must have had words with the old man again, so she said with a smile, "I told you not to go and ask, but you would not believe me and had to go. It is always because your questions are unreasonable that the old gentleman's words give you offense. You must be more broad-minded, and not take the narrow view of a small man." Hearing Yuanzhen's words, Squire Ma's face softened a little, and he said to her, "I thought the old fellow was a man of virtue; who would have guessed he was a covetous devil." Sun Yuanzhen asked, "How do you know he is a covetous man?" So Squire Ma told her the whole of Wang Chongyang's demand for the family fortune. When Sun Yuanzhen had heard it out she said, "There must be some reason why old Mr. Wang asks for your fortune; why did you not ask him plainly? As the saying goes, 'A thousand years of land, eight hundred owners.' Such property is the most impartial thing under heaven and earth; it merely passes through men's hands. Those who know how to use it enjoy it for a few decades, or for a few generations. Those who do not know how to use it are like flowers struck by rain or clouds scattered by wind: no sooner does it come to hand than it melts away, and is in someone else's hands again. That is why it is said that wealth is the common property of the world, turning and passing on in endless circulation. The poor become rich, and the rich become poor; where is the master of a hundred generations, or the miser who keeps his hoard for a thousand years?"
A ten-thousand-string fortune — what is there to boast? / Who can keep it whole, and never see it lost?
Wealth is the common portion of the world below; / can one for a thousand years still hold it so?

Now Sun Yuanzhen exhorted her husband Ma Yu, saying, "Old Mr. Wang must have a reason for asking for our fortune. So long as what he says is reasonable, there is no harm in giving it to him. Besides, we have no son and no daughter, and this fortune will in the end fall into other hands." Before she had finished, Squire Ma laughed and said, "Wife, you say it very easily. My forebears moved from Shaanxi to Shandong, endured every hardship, and bit by bit scraped together this estate. Though I am a man of no worth, I dare not give my ancestors' bitter toil and sweat away to a stranger for nothing. Besides, you and I are only half through our years; if we give the family fortune to another, how shall we live out the rest of our days, and what shall we eat and wear? Would that not ruin the great matter?" Sun Yuanzhen said, "It is in vain that you are a man, and yet so lacking in understanding! We give him our fortune in order to seek from him the Way of long life. Once we have the Way and have cultivated into immortals, what use would the fortune be to us?" She went on, "When one son becomes an immortal, nine generations of ancestors are raised up. How is that failing our forebears? It seems to me that this one word 'Way' is worth far more than your ten-thousand-string fortune."
Gold and silver, treasures like the Ganges' sand, / fall short of what the Way's merit can command;
Treasures, though many, are consumed at last; / the Way's merit through all ages stands fast.

Now when Squire Ma had heard Sun Yuanzhen's words he said, "Wife, your words are not lacking in beauty, but if we fail to become immortals, will it not be a case of trying to paint a tiger and getting a dog instead?" Sun Yuanzhen said, "A man must have constancy. If a man has no constancy, he may not even practice as a shaman or a physician; how much less can he learn to be an immortal! Where there is a will, the thing is done; where there is no will, it is never accomplished. It all depends on whether one has constancy, whether one has will. As the saying goes, 'Immortals were all made from mortal men; the fear is only that the mortal heart is not single.' If only you set your heart on it singly and wholeheartedly, you will naturally get whatever you seek as you wish it. Which of the immortals and buddhas of every age was not a mortal man who cultivated to completion? Could they have been immortals from the womb?" Hearing this, Squire Ma nodded and said it was well said.

The next day he came to the Moon-Inviting Studio to see Wang Chongyang and said, "Yesterday, old sir, you spoke of wanting my family fortune; but I do not know what you mean to use this wealth for." Master Chongyang answered with a solemn face, "It is my wish to gather far and wide the men of the world who cultivate and awaken to the Way, and to have them cultivate and practice the Way here. Your wealth will be taken and used to nourish their natures and protect their practice, so that outwardly they have no entanglements and inwardly they have sustenance, coming in peace and joy and going in gladness." Master Chongyang told Squire Ma his true purpose plainly, and only then was Squire Ma's heart gladdened and won over. But whether he renounced the family fortune or not, hear the next chapter's unfolding.
He who can give his own away and follow what is right / is counted a great sage, beyond the mortal plight.

blocks.text: 06. Sun Yuanzhen Persuades Her Husband to Renounce the Family Fortune; Ma Wenkui Takes a Bribe and Bends to Expedience

inline.s: All dharmas are empty; what is there to gain? / He borrows wealth to guard the Way and the true practice sustain;
For now he turns this thing to timely use; / one day he will drop it all and be set loose.

The story tells that when Master Chongyang had explained to Ma Yu his words about borrowing wealth to guard the Way and gathering cultivators of the Way, Squire Ma was glad and convinced, and said to the master, "By what you say, old sir, you are a man of great virtue and integrity. My humble wife of the Sun family and I both wish to take you, old sir, as our teacher. What does the master think of it?" Chongyang said, "If you and your wife truly mean to cultivate the Way, I have no objection either way. But you must first renounce the family fortune, and only then will I transmit to you the supreme Way, so that you may be single-minded and single-hearted, and not forever entangled and bound." Squire Ma said, "If you, old sir, have need of silver, use it as you will; I am not stingy. Why must it be renounced?" Wang Chongyang said, "If it is not renounced, it remains yours, and I cannot act freely as I please." Squire Ma said, "The land lies outside, the silver within. I will bring the deeds and account books and hand them over to you, old sir; that is renunciation enough." Master Chongyang said, "For the time being keep the deeds with you; you need only invite the clan head to witness and draw up a written deed of renunciation, and that will serve as proof." Squire Ma's joy turned to worry.

He took leave of the master and went back to the main chamber, where he told Sun Yuanzhen what Chongyang had said, adding, "As I see it, this business will not do." Yuanzhen said, "How do you see that it will not do?" Squire Ma said, "Do you not know the hearts of the people of our clan?" Yuanzhen said, "Each man has his own heart; how can one know them all?" Squire Ma said, "The people of our clan see that you and I have no heir and no descendants, and every one of them is waiting to divide the family estate. They are only waiting for the two of us to die, and then the fortune and the land will all be theirs. How would they ever let me renounce the family fortune to an outsider? That is why I say it will not do." Sun Yuanzhen said, "That is no difficulty. Tomorrow invite a few of the influential clan heads to come and talk it over. If they agree, well and good; if they will not consent, you may do thus and so, and they will certainly be glad to comply. I guarantee the matter will be accomplished." Squire Ma laughed when he heard this and said, "Wife, you truly have talent; this business will most likely succeed." He at once called Ma Xing to go and invite the clan heads, to assemble before noon the next day. Of Ma Xing's going to invite the clan heads there is no need to speak.

The next day the clan heads arrived, and with them came a number of their fellows of the same generation and their sons and nephews of the younger generation, all secretly hoping for tables of food and drink. When these people had come into the hall they sat down according to their generations. There was one of the highest generation among them, named Ma Long, a tribute scholar, and Ma Long asked Ma Yu, "What have you to say to us, that you have invited us here today?" Ma Yu said, "In recent years your grandson has often suffered from a little chirping ailment (
jiū jī

, a slight illness, a touch of indisposition): three days well for every two days ill, and one man cannot manage the affairs of a hundred. And more, your grandson's wife is often troubled by dizziness and confusion of the head, and finds it hard to look after matters. Now there is an old gentleman Wang who has come from Shaanxi, an honest and kindly man, whom I have kept in the house. It is my wish to hand over the estate to him to manage, while my wife and I eat the bread of leisure. He agreed readily, but asked that I invite the clan heads to witness and draw up a deed of renunciation for him. That is why I have asked you elders to come and talk it over: let us draw up a deed of renunciation and give it to him." Hardly had Squire Ma stopped speaking when one of his elder cousins, named Ma Ming, was angered. This Ma Ming rose to his feet, pointed at Ma Yu, and said, "Are you a fool? Are you a simpleton? Wild talk! Our ancestral foundation may only be preserved; how can there be any question of giving it away to another? Who has deluded and cajoled you, into what sort of trap have you fallen, that you speak such groundless words?" Squire Ma knew in his heart that his position was unreasonable, and seeing Ma Ming enraged, he dared not speak again.

There was a cousin of his father's generation, Ma Wenkui, a licentiate of the Confucian school (a xiùcai); and there was also an elder cousin, Ma Zhao, a student of the Imperial College (a jiànshēng). These two gentry were the two outstanding men of the Ma clan. In all matters great and small everything depended on the two of them to settle it; whether a thing could be done or not was decided by a single word from them. Ma Wenkui was a man of expedients. Seeing Ma Ming berate Ma Yu, he followed along and said, "Do not blame him. Your squire is an honest man, and blaming him is useless. Go and call that old gentleman Wang out, and let me question him and see what his reason is." Having spoken, he called Ma Xing to go and bring him. Ma Xing was gone only a short while when he brought the old gentleman to the front of the hall. He did not exchange courtesies with anyone, and no one paid him the least regard. At the sight of him Ma Ming laughed aloud and said, "I wondered which Mr. Wang it was; so it is that beggarly lone old man." Ma Wenkui said to Master Chongyang, "You old fellow have begged in our parts for several years, and we have never heard that you had any ability. We do not know what our squire saw in you to take you into the house, where you have clothes and food; that is quite enough. You should have kept to your place and lived out your remaining years in peace. Why have you deluded my nephew and made him renounce the family fortune to you? You are a man of fifty or sixty; you cannot be wholly without sense. Where under heaven is there such a principle? Do you not fear to be laughed at when you say such things?"

When Ma Wenkui had finished, Master Chongyang answered, "All my life I have had no ability; it is only that I have been frightened by poverty, and so I told him to let me have this family fortune, that I might live a few easy years. Let them laugh or not as they please." Before he had finished, Ma Fu and Ma Gui sprang forward and spat (
cuì

, spitting at a man to show contempt) several times in Master Chongyang's face, saying, "You shameless old fellow! A wry-mouthed girl wanting to wear a phoenix crown, a weasel wanting to eat swan's flesh! You have lived fifty or sixty years to no purpose, and now you speak such shameless words; it makes one furious." Ma Fu said to Ma Gui, "Let us not make a clamor; the best plan is simply to drive him out of the village." So saying, they were about to lay hands on him, when Ma Zhao came forward and blocked them, saying, "There is no need to drive him out. Have pity on him as a lone old man; since our squire has kept him, let him be. Only let the squire not renounce the estate, and that is all." Only then did Ma Fu and Ma Gui hold their hands. Squire Ma whispered something or other into the tribute scholar Ma's ear, and Ma Long said to the company, "You youngsters need not make such a clamor; go home, each of you. I have my own decision to make: if I do not let him renounce it, how would he dare?" This old tribute scholar was the senior elder of the whole Ma clan, and who dared disobey him? So each went home.

Squire Ma privately kept back Ma Long, Ma Wenkui, and Ma Zhao, invited them into the study to sit down, and entertained them with wine and food. The old tribute scholar sat at the head; Scholar Ma sat at the lower end to keep him company; the imperial-college scholar Ma sat on the left and Squire Ma on the right. They had no sooner sat down than servants came and went passing cups and bowls, filling the flagon and pouring the wine, with fine dishes and delicacies beyond telling. When three rounds of wine had passed, Squire Ma rose to his feet and said, "My third grandfather, my second uncle, and my elder brother are all here. I, Ma Yu, have a matter on my mind that I wish to discuss with my third grandfather and my second uncle." Scholar Ma said, "Whatever you have to say, say it; we will all turn it over together." Squire Ma said, "Would I really renounce my family property to Wang Chongyang? I would only let him keep watch over it for me for a few years, so that I may get a little leisure." Ma Zhao said, "Letting him keep watch is no great matter; but why draw up a deed of renunciation?" Squire Ma said, "Elder brother, you do not understand. This is nothing but a temporary expedient: I want to make him wholeheartedly and sincerely keep watch for me, so that I can be at ease and he will not grow slack." Ma Wenkui said, "Your reasoning I do not understand; tell it to me slowly." Squire Ma said, "Second uncle, hear your nephew out. It is only that your nephew is much afflicted with illness, and your nephew's wife too is often troubled with dizziness, so that she finds it hard to manage affairs. For a long time I have wished to find an honest, loyal man to run things for me. Happily heaven has answered my wish, and this old gentleman Wang has come, a man of the utmost honesty and loyalty. I had a mind to hand the estate over to him to manage, and so I said to him, 'Manage this household well, and treat it as though it were your own estate; do not be of two minds.' The old gentleman did not know how to take a hint, and asked me straight out, 'You tell me to treat this fortune as my own; do you mean to renounce it to me?' Seeing him talk such foolish talk, I answered him in his own foolish vein: 'Renounce it to you? Renounce it to you, then; what does it matter?' It was plainly a joke, but he took it for the truth and demanded that I invite the clan heads to witness and draw up a written deed of renunciation for him. I reckon that he is a lone man with no close kin, no relatives or friends; even if I renounce it to him, he cannot carry it off anywhere. Besides, he is advanced in years; how many more years can he live? Let me draw up a deed for him and win his goodwill, so that he will manage things for me with single-hearted devotion, while I enjoy some leisure and nurse my illness. When he dies, the fortune comes back to me. What loss is there in it? I beg my second uncle to decide for me and bring this matter to completion."
